text: A file written on one machine displays as `cafÃ©` on another. What happened?
choices: The file was corrupted in transfer, and the two extra characters are damaged bytes.
It was written as UTF-8 and read as a single-byte encoding, so the two bytes of é were decoded as two separate characters.
The file was written as UTF-16 and read as UTF-8, so each character gained a null byte.
The receiving machine lacks a font containing é, so it substituted the nearest available glyphs.
explanation: The bytes C3 A9 are é in UTF-8 and Ã followed by © in Latin-1. Nothing was corrupted and nothing threw, because Latin-1 assigns a character to all 256 byte values and therefore has no invalid input. The pattern is called mojibake, and recognising that it means "UTF-8 read as a single-byte encoding" will save you an afternoon at some point.
